title: Punctuation and commands
goal: Look up the stroke for any punctuation mark, symbol, capital, cursor move, editing key or shortcut, and what each does to the spacing around it.

blocks.x: How punctuation strokes work

Punctuation lives in `rules/reserved/punctuation.json`: **200 strokes**. 144 are forked from Plover's punctuation dictionary, 4 are hyphen and dash strokes from [Lapwing chapter 20](https://lapwing.aerick.ca/Chapter-20.html), and 52 are the glued fingerspelling letters (listed on [the fingerspelling page](#/ref/fingerspelling/fingerspelling-in-running-text)). Commands live in `rules/reserved/commands.json`: **84 strokes** ([below](#/ref/punctuation/commands)). All of them are [reserved](#/ref/reserved-strokes): no word takes them.

Most marks have several strokes, one for each situation: plain, struck twice, with glue before or after so no unwanted space appears, after a quote, before a parenthesis. The **Plover code** column is what the stroke sends.

head: Code
Meaning
rows: attach to the neighbouring word: no space on that side (`{^x}` attaches to the word before, `{x^}` to the word after, `{^x^}` both)
carry a pending capital past the mark: the next word is still capitalized
glue: the text joins the previous glued text (used for fingerspelled letters)

blocks.x: A name is written two ways. The ordinary one: the word's ordinary outline, capitalized by `KPA` before it. The [name lane](#/ref/names): the stroke `#` alone, then the same outline, which types the name capitalized in one go (`#/TKAPBL` is *Daniel*), with a names-only solver behind it for a name the dictionary lacks. Glued fingerspelled letters

The other 52 strokes in `punctuation.json` are the glued letters `A*` a, `A*P` A, and so on for the whole alphabet. They are listed in full, with the rule, on [the fingerspelling page](#/ref/fingerspelling/fingerspelling-in-running-text).
Commands

86 strokes in `rules/reserved/commands.json`. The `STPH` movement family and the F-keys are Lapwing's own strokes, minus its number-key variants (lyk has no number key). Lapwing's repeated-arrow chords (such as `STPH-RS`, Left twice) and its Plover-only commands (`{PLOVER:CONFIGURE}`, `{MODE:CAPS}`) were left out. There is no caps-lock: for a run of words in capitals, strike [[KPA*L]] before each word. 29 of them (the cursor and selection family, Backspace, and the toggle, show and hide controls of the overlay, tape, keyboard and lookup) send on the first key up: see [Send on the first key up](#/ref/punctuation/send-on-the-first-key-up).

blocks.x: Send on the first key up

A stroke normally goes when its **last** key comes up. A dictionary entry that carries the marker `{:firstup}` goes when its **first** key comes up instead, and the keys still down **wait**: the next key you press makes a new stroke with them. So you hold most of a chord and tap one key, again and again, and each tap is a stroke. Letting go of the held keys alone sends nothing.

Example: hold `STPH` (the left hand) and tap `-R` three times. That is [[STPH-R]] three times, Left, Left, Left. Without lifting the left hand, tap `-P`: [[STPH-P]], Up. Hold `*` as well and the same taps select ([[STPH*R]], Shift+Left). The rule for every entry below is the same: hold all but one key of the stroke, tap the last. In an entry the marker sits **in front of** the command and the `{^}`, `{:firstup}{#Left}{^}`, never after, so Plover reads the rest of it the same way. The marker types nothing and changes no spacing.

blocks.x: **Why these:** each is a command whose natural use is to be repeated, the family shares one left-hand base so a held `STPH` is a cursor chord, and the key sets work out: hold the base plus all but one key, and the held keys plus the tapped key make exactly the next stroke of the family. Holding more keys changes the family in place: `STPH-R` to `STPH-RB` (word left) when you add `-B`, `STPH-R` to `STPH*R` (select) when you add `*`; both are first-up too, so the walk never has to stop. The controls follow the same idea: a toggle, a show or a hide is a state you flip and want to flip again without lifting the hand, and the overlay controls share the base `PHRO*L` the way the cursor family shares `STPH`. In their entries the marker comes first, then `{:transparent}`, then the command: `{:firstup}{:transparent}{:overlay:toggle}`. Keymux reads each marker wherever it stands in the entry, so the order is a convention that keeps the command last.
**Left out on purpose:**

head: Entry
Why it does not carry the marker
rows: Everything that types text: words, briefs, phrases, suffixes
Sending early would send a half-struck word, and a held key would then join the next word. Never.
Punctuation, capitals, glued letters, the retro commands (`{*?}`, `{*<}`, `{>}`)
They change spacing or capitalisation, or act on the previous words; repeating or sending them early is a mistake, not a convenience.
Return submits forms and chat boxes and Escape cancels things: you want the deliberate send of a stroke that has fully come up, and repeating them is rarely wanted.

Wanted repeated, but both strokes sit inside the keys of dozens of common words (89 and 26 words among the 5,000 most common: *taken*, *goodbye*, *girls*, *details*), and they are struck mid-sentence between words. Backspace has the same exposure (14 and 32) but is the key held most often, so it carries the marker.
83 and 38 common words contain these keys (*girl*, *together*, *forward*), and `TPW` is the F-key base, so holding it taps into F-keys. Browser history is a deliberate step, not a repeat.
F1 to F12 and the clipboard and Super shortcuts (`KHR*F`, `KPH*F` and the rest)
Each is its own chord with no shared base, so there is no stroke to hold and tap. Nothing repeats usefully.
They are engine commands that run once.
[[PHRO*TZ]] (clear the tape), [[PHRO*PLZ]] (free the engine from RAM)
Destructive or one-shot: clearing twice is the same as once, and unloading the engine should be a deliberate stroke that has fully come up, not the first key of a chord. Both stay on the last key up.

Opening an open lookup does nothing, so there is nothing to repeat, and the stroke is the widest of the controls: 18 of the 5,000 most common words have a stroke that contains it, and 11 more start with such a stroke, against 2 to 5 for the toggles. Use [[PHR*UP]] to flip the lookup when you want the hold-and-tap.

blocks.x: **The trap.** Keys still down when a first-up stroke goes join the next stroke. Lift the whole hand between a cursor move and the next word, as you do between any two strokes; if one finger lags, that key rides into the next stroke. Likewise, a word whose stroke is a first-up stroke plus more keys is only hit if a key of it lands after another key has already come up, which a chord struck together never does. The exposure among the 5,000 most common words is small: 3 for `STPH-R` and `STPH-RB` (*insurance*, *internal*), 15 to 19 for `STPH-P` `-B` `-G`, 0 to 6 for the rest of the family, 14 and 32 for Backspace. The new controls, counted as the words whose single stroke contains the control's keys plus the longer words whose first stroke does: 3 for `PHRO*L`, 0 for `PHRO*LS` and `PHRO*LD`, 1 for `PHRO*T`, 5 for `PHRO*B` (*belong*, *belongs*, *belonged*, *unbelievable*, *balloon*), 4 for `PHR*UP`, 2 for `PHRUPD`; none of them is a word you type in a hurry.
What runs it

Sending on the first key up is Keymux's. A dictionary entry carrying `{:firstup}` is flagged by Keymux's translator, and its engine sends the stroke when the first key comes up. Setting `disable_first_up: true` in Keymux's config ignores the marker everywhere, and every stroke then goes on the last key up like any other. Dictionaries without the marker, such as the plain Lapwing one, behave as before.

**Plover itself does not know `{:firstup}`.** Plover reads `{:name}` as a call to a registered meta plugin and looks the name up; there is none called `firstup`, and Plover 5.4.2's lookup raises `KeyError: 'firstup'`. So in plain Plover the 29 strokes above would error instead of acting; every other stroke is unaffected. The marker is harmless only in an engine that knows it. lyk is deployed to Keymux, so the 29 strokes carry it; a Plover user can register a one-line meta plugin named `firstup` that does nothing, or take a copy of `commands.json` with the marker removed. The strokes themselves never change either way.

These are reserved like any command: a word can never take a stroke the steno engine itself depends on.
Overlay and lookup controls (Keymux)

Keymux's overlay (the keyboard diagram and the tape) and its live lookup can be shown, hidden and flipped from a stroke. Each stroke below types nothing, keeps the spacing and capitals around it, runs once and stays off the tape. **They act only on an overlay that is already running, and only for now:** nothing is written to the config, and they never start the overlay or change how it starts. Restart it and it comes back as the config says. With no overlay running (or `enabled: false`) they do nothing, with no error.

blocks.x: **How they were chosen.** The six overlay strokes share the base `PHRO*` of the Plover control strokes above, and the last keys name the part and the verb: `-L` the panel (layer), `-T` the tape, `-B` the board (keyboard); a bare part flips it, `S` adds show, `D` adds dismiss (hide), `Z` adds zap (clear). The lookup strokes keep the `PHR-UP` of the lookup command: the plain chord opens, the star flips, `D` closes. Only toggle is given to the tape and keyboard, and show/hide only to the whole panel, to keep the layout small: a hide is a toggle when you know the state. Keymux also parses `{:tape:show}`, `{:tape:hide}`, `{:keyboard:show}`, `{:keyboard:hide}`, `{:overlay:...}` and `{:lookup:open}` for hand-written entries. All nine overlay and lookup strokes are checked free of every word outline, backup and phrase in the built dictionary. **First-up:** seven of the nine carry `{:firstup}` (see [Send on the first key up](#/ref/punctuation/send-on-the-first-key-up)); `PHRO*TZ` and `PHRUP` do not, for the reasons given there.

blocks.x: The big lyk dictionaries take hundreds of megabytes while loaded (about 700 MB). This stroke frees them. **There is no reload stroke:** the next stroke of any kind loads the engine again first and then performs, so the one stroke after an unload is slower (the load time) and nothing is lost. It types nothing, keeps the spacing and capitals around it and stays off the tape, like the controls above. It is runtime-only: nothing is written to the config, and a restart loads the dictionaries as usual. It needs a Keymux that knows `{:engine:unload}`. The outline is the `PHRO*` control base with `-PL` (memory, as in the M of *memory*) and `Z` (zap, as in `PHRO*TZ`); the bare `PHRO*PL` is not used because it begins a multi-stroke word, so a standalone stroke would hold it up.
The transparent marker

A stroke that carries `{:transparent}` is invisible to the translation history. A lookup in the middle of a multi-stroke join no longer breaks it: `THAS`, [[PHRUP]], then `+EUFG` still joins as if the lookup had not been struck, and `*` after the lookup skips straight past it. Keymux treats an entry that is exactly `{plover:lookup}` as transparent already; the marker makes it explicit, and the other controls need it. The marker sits **in front of** the command, like `{:firstup}`, types nothing and changes no spacing. Related markers Keymux defines, not used by any lyk stroke: `{:barrier}` (end any join here), `{:nobarrier}`, and `{:back}` (erase and let undo bring it back).

Four more Keymux-only commands act on the typing history. None needs the overlay.

blocks.x: The undo stroke

The lone `*` (the star key struck by itself) is the undo stroke, and lyk defines it: `*` is `{:undo_or:Control_L(BackSpace)}`. It takes back the last real stroke, exactly as Plover's `*` does (the undone strokes can be put back with [[R*EUD]]; transparent strokes such as the overlay controls are skipped; a held `*` repeats one undo per repeat). The difference is at a **barrier**: after an arrow, Home/End, Page Up/Down, Delete or Escape, a Backspace or Delete word operation, or any shortcut with Ctrl, Alt or Super, the text before the cursor move is no longer next to the cursor, so taking it back would delete text somewhere else. There `*` does not undo: it sends **Ctrl+Backspace** instead (delete a word at the cursor), uses the barrier up and forgets what was before it. The next `*` is an ordinary undo again, of the strokes struck after the barrier. With nothing left to undo at all, `*` also sends Ctrl+Backspace. Keymux decides this (the steno-layer setting `undo_stops_at_barrier`, on by default); lyk only chooses the stroke and the fallback keys. **It needs Keymux commit 137459d or later.**

head: Stroke
Definition
Effect
rows: Undo the last real stroke; at a barrier, or with nothing to undo, Ctrl+Backspace

Plain undo, no fallback: at a barrier or with nothing to undo it does what Keymux's plain undo does there (with `undo_stops_at_barrier` on, that is also Ctrl+Backspace once). Use it to keep the old behaviour of `*` under a name of its own

blocks.x: [[TK*UPS]] is the undo family beside [[TK*UP]] (undo a word): the `-S` is the plain, single step. Keymux also accepts `{:undo_or:ctrl+backspace}` as an alias; lyk writes the canonical form. To change the fallback, edit the one `"*"` line in `rules/reserved/commands.json` (for example `{:undo_or:Escape}` for undo-else-Escape).
In plain Plover

**Plover does not know these metas.** Plover reads `{:name}` as a registered meta plugin and raises `KeyError` (as for `{:firstup}`) for `transparent`, `overlay`, `tape`, `keyboard`, `lookup`, `engine`, `undo_or`, `redo`, `undo_word`, `again` and `swap`. In plain Plover those 15 strokes would error instead of acting; every other stroke is unaffected. **The one that matters is `*`**, the most-used key: its `{:undo_or:...}` meta raises a `KeyError` in plain Plover, so the lone `*` would not undo. Workarounds: use a copy of `commands.json` with `"*": "=undo"` (Plover's own undo) and the other 14 entries removed (for [[PHRUP]] only the `{:transparent}` marker: `{PLOVER:LOOKUP}` is plain Plover), or register no-op meta plugins with those names (fine for the overlay, which does not exist there; a no-op `undo_or` leaves `*` dead). The theory is not changed for Plover; Keymux is the target engine.
